text:
The most visible part of a regional electricity market is the transmission line. The most important part may be everything that has to work after it is built.

Our research looks at the gap between completing an African power interconnector and creating a functioning electricity market.

A line creates the technical option to trade. Reliable trade requires much more: synchronised systems, market rules, dispatch, transmission tariffs, creditworthy buyers, payment security, foreign-exchange settlement, sufficient supply and demand, national-grid capacity, local distribution and maintenance.

The numbers show why that distinction matters.

More than 4,000 kilometres of high-voltage transmission connect the grids of 15 West African countries, yet the World Bank estimated that only about 8% of the region's electricity was traded across borders in May 2026.

In Southern Africa, competitive markets are established, but bilateral contracts still dominate. In June 2026, 47 GWh of matched energy across SAPP markets could not be traded because of transmission constraints.

Eastern Africa shows another version of the same issue: substantial bilateral cross-border trade, but no recorded energy on the central market platform as of May 2026.

None of this says regional integration is failing. It says the problem is changing.

StoneComms proposes a Corridor Readiness Ledger that tests seven linked conditions: physical completion, synchronisation, market rules, settlement, supply and demand, national and local delivery, and long-term governance and maintenance.

The useful question for investors is no longer simply “is the line finished?” It is “which missing span still prevents this corridor from delivering reliable, paid-for electricity?”

Read the research:
https://stonecomms.com/research/missing-span-africa-power-interconnectors-electricity-markets

As African power pools deepen, which constraint deserves more attention: transmission capacity, payment security, market liquidity or national-grid readiness?
